questions.knowledge_point: Applying Properties of the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,(3+2\text{i})b+c⟩$ if  

$\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=2\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨c,a⟩=1+\text{i}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,\,(3+2\text{i})b+c⟩ & =⟨a,(3+2\text{i})b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =(\overset{―}{3+2\text{i}})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =(3-2\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3-2\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ & =(3-2\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨c,a⟩:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(3-2\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+\overset{―}{⟨c,a⟩} & =(3-2\text{i})\cdot \overset{―}{2\text{i}}+\overset{―}{1+\text{i}} \\  & =(3-2\text{i})\cdot (-2\text{i})+(1-\text{i}) \\  & =-6\text{i}+4{\text{i}}^{2}+1-\text{i} \\  & =-6\text{i}+4(-1)+1-\text{i} \\  & =-3-7\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩$ if  

$\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=-1-\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩ & =⟨a,(4-\text{i})b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =(\overset{―}{4-\text{i}})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =(4+\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4+\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c\text{ }⟩ & =(4+\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$  

$$
\begin{aligned}(4+\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩ & =(4+\text{i})\cdot (\overset{―}{-1-\text{i}})+5 \\  & =(4+\text{i})\cdot (-1+\text{i})+5 \\  & =-5+3\text{i}+5 \\  & =3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$
- $⟨a,a⟩>0$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that if $a=0$ then $⟨a,a⟩=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Hermitian Inner Product
questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨a,0⟩=0$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
- $2⟨a,b⟩=⟨a,-2b⟩$ for any  $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,b⟩\in R$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. By the antilinearity in the second argument we have that  

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,0⟩ & =⟨a,0\cdot 0⟩=\overset{―}{0}⟨a,0⟩=0⟨a,0⟩=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,-2b⟩=\overset{―}{(-2)}⟨a,b⟩=-2⟨a,b⟩\ne 2⟨a,b⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number, in general.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

- $⟨a,-ia⟩=-i⟨a,a⟩$ for any nonzero vector  $a\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
- $⟨a,b⟩\in R$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false.  By the antilinearity of $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$  in the second argument we have 

$$
⟨a,-ia⟩=\overset{―}{(-i)}⟨a,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\ne -i⟨a,a⟩
$$

 
for any nonzero vector  $a\in {C}^{n}.$

- Statement II  is true. Indeed, the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

- Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number in general.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
